Dumped Cherries a Reminder of Awfulness of USDA Marketing Orders

"Such government-mandated waste is an outrage. Worse still, the excess cherries, Santucci notes, can't be given away or donated."

I don't understand this part, can anyone shed some light as to why this rule exists?

Farmers back in the day convinced the USDA to create cartels for various goods like cherries, raisins, etc. They claimed that if the government artificially suppressed supply by limiting how much of specific types of produce, everyone would be better off and rainbows would fly out our asses. This includes forcing farmers to destroy "excess" production.

What this actually does is create a cartel so that the incumbent producers have no competition and can bone consumers with higher prices. It's as retarded as it sounds.

What if we steal them from him? like, he explicitly forbids us from taking these excess cherries from him, and then goes to do something important, like write a letter to tell these jerks how retarded they are. and then we just... take the extra cherries from him. against his will.
Because giving them away would reduce demand and thus, reduce the price.
Giving a food bank or shelter cherries would hardly reduce the price; in California I know a lot of farmers that donate "extra" food without reducing the price of said item.

I don't agree with it, but that's the logic that was used. I think giving the extra food to homeless shelters is wonderful and since it goes to people who wouldn't be buying food anyways, it doesn't disrupt affect the market.

The farmer cartels @daskapitalist describes exist to stabilize the price of a good so that farmers aren't hung out to dry when the crop they spent time and money growing is worth less than what they invested to grow it.

Imagine growing a crop you spent thousands on seeds, months fertilizing, tilling, watering, and because they produced so well the price plummets and you can't recoup your investment selling it all (if you could sell it all).

I'm sure there is corruption and profiteering but the original motive for such arrangements reduces risk for famers and helps to stabilize the food supply.
